::: {.solutions}

The floor $\lfloor x\rfloor$ and ceiling $\lceil x\rceil$ turn a smooth expression into a **staircase** —
constant on each unit interval, jumping by $1$ at the integers. Almost every TMUA/MAT question about them is
really "add up the steps", and this clinic drills exactly that, from the TMUA papers and the MAT.

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 1 · Floor, ceiling &amp; fractional part</div>
<div class="fs-title">Step Functions — Exam Skim Sheet</div>
<div class="fs-sub">On each interval between consecutive integers the bracket is a constant. Everything follows from that.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### 1 · Floor $\lfloor x\rfloor$
Round **down** — the largest integer $\le x$.

$\lfloor 3.7\rfloor=3$, and — the trap — $\lfloor-2.3\rfloor=\mathbf{-3}$ (further from $0$, **not** $-2$).
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 2 · Ceiling $\lceil x\rceil$
Round **up** — the smallest integer $\ge x$.

$\lceil3.2\rceil=4$, $\lceil-2.3\rceil=-2$.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 3 · Fractional part
$\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$, always in $[0,1)$.

[It is what the floor threw away.]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 4 · How the two relate
For a **non-integer**, $\lceil x\rceil=\lfloor x\rfloor+1$.

At an integer they are **equal**.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 5 · The one idea
Between consecutive integers the bracket is **constant**, so the graph is a **staircase** and an integral is a **sum of rectangular strips**.

[Turn every step integral into $\sum(\text{height}\times\text{width})$.]{.eg}
:::

::::

:::::

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to attack **any** floor/ceiling problem

| If you are asked to… | The reliable move | Section |
|---|---|---|
| **evaluate** $\lfloor x\rfloor,\lceil x\rceil,\{x\}$ | round down / up; watch negatives | §1 |
| **integrate** $\int\lfloor x\rfloor$, $\int g(\lfloor x\rfloor)$ | constant on each unit strip → **sum the strip areas** | §2 |
| a strip sum that **grows geometrically** | it's a **geometric series** $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ or $\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ | §2 |
| a **finite sum** $\sum\lfloor f(k)\rfloor$ | group the $k$ that share the same floor value | §3 |
| **count solutions** of an equation with $\lfloor x\rfloor$ | write $\lfloor x\rfloor=n$ (integer) and solve on each strip | §3 |

**One idea covers all of it:** *the bracket is constant on each unit interval — replace it by that constant
and add up.*
:::

**On this page:** 1. Reading floor, ceiling & fractional part · 2. Integrating step functions · 3. Sums &
counting · 4. Harder step integrals

## 1 · Reading floor, ceiling & fractional part

### Question 1

::: {.question}
Evaluate $\lfloor3.7\rfloor$, $\lceil3.7\rceil$, $\lfloor-2.3\rfloor$, $\lceil-2.3\rceil$, and $\{-2.3\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(warm-up — mind the negatives)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — round down / up correctly, especially for negatives
:::

**Answer: $3,\ 4,\ -3,\ -2,\ 0.7$.**

- $\lfloor3.7\rfloor=3$ (down), $\lceil3.7\rceil=4$ (up).
- $\lfloor-2.3\rfloor=\mathbf{-3}$ — "down" means **more negative** (the largest integer $\le-2.3$ is $-3$).
- $\lceil-2.3\rceil=-2$ (the smallest integer $\ge-2.3$).
- $\{-2.3\}=(-2.3)-\lfloor-2.3\rfloor=(-2.3)-(-3)=0.7$ — a fractional part is always in $[0,1)$, even for
  negatives.
:::

:::

## 2 · Integrating step functions

::: {.callout-tip}
## Concept — an integral of a bracket is a sum of strips

On $[n,\,n+1)$, $\lfloor x\rfloor=n$ (and on $(n-1,\,n]$, $\lceil x\rceil=n$) — a **constant**. So
$\displaystyle\int$ of a bracket is a **sum of rectangles**: width $\times$ (the constant value). Two standard
results:
$$\int_0^n\lfloor x\rfloor\,\mathrm dx=0+1+\dots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}2,\qquad
\int_0^n\lceil x\rceil\,\mathrm dx=1+2+\dots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2.$$
:::

### Question 2

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_0^5\lfloor x\rfloor\,\mathrm dx$ and $\displaystyle\int_0^5\lceil x\rceil\,\mathrm dx$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the two fundamental step integrals)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — build $\int\lfloor x\rfloor$ and $\int\lceil x\rceil$ from strips
:::

**Answer: $10$ and $15$.**

$\lfloor x\rfloor$ takes the values $0,1,2,3,4$ on the five unit strips $[0,1),\dots,[4,5)$, so the integral is
$0+1+2+3+4=10=\tfrac{5\cdot4}2$. Meanwhile $\lceil x\rceil$ takes $1,2,3,4,5$ on $(0,1],\dots,(4,5]$, giving
$1+2+3+4+5=15=\tfrac{5\cdot6}2$.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(6.6,2.9))
for n in range(5):
    ax[0].plot([n,n+1],[n,n],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2); ax[0].fill_between([n,n+1],[n,n],color='#2b6cb0',alpha=0.12)
    ax[1].plot([n,n+1],[n+1,n+1],color='#dd6b20',lw=2); ax[1].fill_between([n,n+1],[n+1,n+1],color='#dd6b20',alpha=0.12)
ax[0].set_title('⌊x⌋: strips 0,1,2,3,4 → 10',fontsize=9); ax[1].set_title('⌈x⌉: strips 1,2,3,4,5 → 15',fontsize=9)
for a in ax: a.set_xlim(0,5); a.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

### Question 3

::: {.question}
Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}x\lfloor x\rfloor\,\mathrm dx$. &nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac{26}3$
&nbsp; **B** $\tfrac{11\pi^2}8-\tfrac{13}2$ &nbsp; **C** $\tfrac{11\pi^2}8$ &nbsp; **D** $\tfrac{7\pi^3}{24}$
&nbsp; **E** $\tfrac{7\pi^3}{24}-\tfrac{13}8$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Tyler Mock TMUA, Set C — a variable coefficient)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\int x\lfloor x\rfloor$: split where the floor jumps, integrate $x$ on each piece
:::

**Answer: B ($\tfrac{11\pi^2}8-\tfrac{13}2$).**

**Step 1 — where does $\lfloor x\rfloor$ jump?** On $[\tfrac\pi2,\pi]\approx[1.57,3.14]$: $\lfloor
x\rfloor=1$ on $[\tfrac\pi2,2)$, $=2$ on $[2,3)$, $=3$ on $[3,\pi]$.

**Step 2 — integrate $x\lfloor x\rfloor$ piece by piece** (only the *constant* floor changes, the $x$ is
ordinary):
$$\int_{\pi/2}^{2}\!x\,\mathrm dx+2\!\int_{2}^{3}\!x\,\mathrm dx+3\!\int_{3}^{\pi}\!x\,\mathrm dx
=\Big(2-\tfrac{\pi^2}8\Big)+2\cdot\tfrac52+3\cdot\tfrac{\pi^2-9}2.$$

**Step 3 — collect.** $=2-\tfrac{\pi^2}8+5+\tfrac{3\pi^2-27}2=\dfrac{11\pi^2}8-\dfrac{13}2.$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 4

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{99}2^{\lceil x\rceil}\,\mathrm dx$. &nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $2^{99}$ &nbsp;
**B** $2^{99}-1$ &nbsp; **C** $2^{99}-2$ &nbsp; **D** $2^{100}$ &nbsp; **E** $2^{100}-1$ &nbsp;
**F** $2^{100}-2$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(TMUA 2023 P2 Q17 — a geometric strip sum)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $2^{\lceil x\rceil}$ is constant on each strip; the strips form a geometric series
:::

**Answer: F ($2^{100}-2$).**

**Step 1 — constant on each strip.** On $(n-1,\,n]$, $\lceil x\rceil=n$, so $2^{\lceil x\rceil}=2^{n}$ is
constant there ($n=1,\dots,99$), each strip of width $1$.

**Step 2 — sum the geometric series.**
$$\int_{0}^{99}2^{\lceil x\rceil}\,\mathrm dx=\sum_{n=1}^{99}2^{n}=2+2^{2}+\dots+2^{99}=2\!\left(2^{99}-1
\right)=2^{100}-2.$$

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.0))
for n in range(1,6):
    plt.plot([n-1,n],[2**n,2**n],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
    plt.plot([n,n],[2**n,2**(n+1)],color='#2b6cb0',lw=0.6,ls=':')
plt.xticks(range(0,6)); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('2^⌈x⌉'); plt.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.title('constant 2ⁿ on (n−1, n]; strips double each step',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 5

::: {.question}
Define $\mathrm f(x)=\left(\tfrac34\right)^{\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor}$ for $0<x<2$, and $\mathrm f(x)=0$
otherwise. Find $\displaystyle\int_0^2\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$. &nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** $1$ &nbsp; **(b)** $2$
&nbsp; **(c)** $3$ &nbsp; **(d)** $4$ &nbsp; **(e)** $5$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(MAT 2023 Q1J — a floor inside a log)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor$ is constant on $[2^m,2^{m+1})$; strips form a geometric series
:::

**Answer: (c) $3$.**

**Step 1 — where is the floor constant?** $\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor=m$ exactly on $x\in[2^{m},2^{m+1})$. For
$0<x<2$ this uses $m=0,-1,-2,\dots$, and $\mathrm f$ is the constant $\left(\tfrac34\right)^{m}$ there.

**Step 2 — strip areas.** The interval for $m=-k$ ($k\ge0$) is $[2^{-k},2^{-k+1})$, width $2^{-k}$, height
$\left(\tfrac43\right)^{k}$; area $=\left(\tfrac43\right)^{k}2^{-k}=\left(\tfrac23\right)^{k}$.

**Step 3 — geometric series.** $\displaystyle\int_0^2\mathrm f=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\tfrac23\right)^{k}
=\dfrac1{1-\frac23}=3.$

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.0))
for k in range(0,6):
    lo,hi=2.0**(-k),2.0**(-k+1); h=(4/3)**k
    plt.plot([lo,hi],[h,h],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.xlim(0,2); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('f(x)'); plt.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.title('constant on each interval; strip areas (2/3)^k sum to 3',fontsize=8.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 6

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_0^4\{x\}\,\mathrm dx$, where $\{x\}$ is the fractional part of $x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the fractional part)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$ repeats the same sawtooth on every unit interval
:::

**Answer: $2$.**

On each unit interval $[n,n+1)$, $\{x\}=x-n$ runs from $0$ up to $1$ — a triangle of area $\tfrac12$. There are
$4$ such identical triangles on $[0,4]$, so $\displaystyle\int_0^4\{x\}\,\mathrm dx=4\times\tfrac12=2$. *(In
general $\int_0^n\{x\}\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac n2$.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## 3 · Sums & counting

### Question 7

::: {.question}
Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}\big\lfloor\sqrt k\big\rfloor$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a finite floor sum)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — group the terms that share the same floor value
:::

**Answer: $19$.**

Group by the value of $\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor$:

- $\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor=1$ for $k=1,2,3$ (since $1\le\sqrt k<2$) — that's $3$ terms of $1$.
- $\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor=2$ for $k=4,\dots,8$ ($2\le\sqrt k<3$) — $5$ terms of $2$.
- $\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor=3$ for $k=9,10$ — $2$ terms of $3$.

Total $=3(1)+5(2)+2(3)=3+10+6=19$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 8

::: {.question}
How many real solutions does $\;\lfloor x\rfloor=x^{2}-2\;$ have?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(count solutions with a floor)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — set $\lfloor x\rfloor=n$ (an integer), solve on each strip, keep the ones that land in it
:::

**Answer: $2$.**

**Step 1 — the right side must be an integer.** $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is an integer, so $x^{2}-2=n$ for some
integer $n$, i.e. $x=\pm\sqrt{n+2}$; and this must satisfy $\lfloor x\rfloor=n$.

**Step 2 — test each strip.** Try small $n$:

- $n=-1$: $x^{2}=1\Rightarrow x=\pm1$. Need $\lfloor x\rfloor=-1$: $x=-1$ gives $\lfloor-1\rfloor=-1$ ✔;
  $x=1$ gives $\lfloor1\rfloor=1\ne-1$ ✘.
- $n=0$: $x=\pm\sqrt2\approx\pm1.41$. Need $\lfloor x\rfloor=0$: neither works ($\lfloor1.41\rfloor=1$,
  $\lfloor-1.41\rfloor=-2$).
- $n=2$: $x=\pm2$. Need $\lfloor x\rfloor=2$: $x=2$ gives $\lfloor2\rfloor=2$ ✔; $x=-2$ ✘.
- other $n$ give no landing root.

So the solutions are $x=-1$ and $x=2$ — **two**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-2.5,2.5,1000)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.8,3.2))
plt.plot(x,x**2-2,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y=x²−2')
xs=np.linspace(-3,3,1000); plt.plot(xs,np.floor(xs),color='#dd6b20',lw=1.5,label='y=⌊x⌋',drawstyle='steps-post')
for r in (-1,2): plt.plot(r,r**2-2,'o',color='crimson')
plt.ylim(-3,5); plt.xlim(-2.5,2.5); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title('⌊x⌋ = x²−2 meets at x=−1 and x=2',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## 4 · Harder step integrals

::: {.callout-tip}
## Concept — harder brackets, same idea

The staircase move still works when the bracket is **squared** ($\lfloor x\rfloor^{2}$), **multiplied by a
variable** ($x\lfloor x\rfloor$, $\lfloor x\rfloor\{x\}$), or **applied to a curved inside** ($\lceil
x^{2}\rceil$, $\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor$). The only new skill: for a curved inside, **split where the inside
crosses each integer** — those split points may be **irrational** ($\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$, …). On each piece the
bracket is a constant; integrate the rest of the integrand there.
:::

### Question 9

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}\lfloor x\rfloor^{2}\,\mathrm dx$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the bracket squared)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\lfloor x\rfloor^{2}$ is $0,1,4,9,\dots$ on the strips
:::

**Answer: $14$.**

On the strips $[0,1),[1,2),[2,3),[3,4)$ the value $\lfloor x\rfloor^{2}$ is $0^{2},1^{2},2^{2},3^{2}$, each
over width $1$:
$$\int_0^4\lfloor x\rfloor^{2}\,\mathrm dx=0+1+4+9=14.$$

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.figure(figsize=(4.8,2.8))
for n in range(4):
    plt.plot([n,n+1],[n**2,n**2],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2); plt.fill_between([n,n+1],[n**2,n**2],color='#2b6cb0',alpha=0.12)
plt.xlim(0,4); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.title('⌊x⌋²: strips 0,1,4,9 → 14',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 10

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{n}2^{\lfloor x\rfloor}\,\mathrm dx$ (for a positive integer $n$), and evaluate it
at $n=5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the floor version of the geometric strip sum)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $2^{\lfloor x\rfloor}$ vs $2^{\lceil x\rceil}$ — which power on which strip?
:::

**Answer: $2^{n}-1$; at $n=5$ it is $31$.**

On $[k,\,k+1)$, $\lfloor x\rfloor=k$, so $2^{\lfloor x\rfloor}=2^{k}$ for $k=0,1,\dots,n-1$:
$$\int_0^n 2^{\lfloor x\rfloor}\,\mathrm dx=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{k}=2^{n}-1.$$
*(Compare $\int_0^{n}2^{\lceil x\rceil}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}2^{k}=2^{n+1}-2$: the **ceiling** starts one power
higher because $\lceil x\rceil$ takes $1,\dots,n$ instead of $0,\dots,n-1$.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 11

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{16}\big\lfloor\log_2 x\big\rfloor\,\mathrm dx$. &nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $15$ &nbsp;
**B** $26$ &nbsp; **C** $34$ &nbsp; **D** $42$ &nbsp; **E** $49$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a floor of a log — widths that grow)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor=k$ on $[2^{k},2^{k+1})$, so the strips **widen**
:::

**Answer: C ($34$).**

$\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor=k$ on $[2^{k},2^{k+1})$, a strip of **width $2^{k}$**. On $[1,16)$:

| interval | $[1,2)$ | $[2,4)$ | $[4,8)$ | $[8,16)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| value $k$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| width | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ |

$$\int_1^{16}\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor\,\mathrm dx=0\cdot1+1\cdot2+2\cdot4+3\cdot8=0+2+8+24=34.$$

**Where the wrong options come from.** Using width $1$ for every strip (as if the integers were evenly
spaced) gives $0+1+2+3=6$, then scaling wrongly — the point is the widths **double** each time.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 12

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}\lfloor x\rfloor\,\mathrm dx$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a negative range — the sign trap)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\lfloor x\rfloor$ on negative strips is $-1,-2,\dots$
:::

**Answer: $0$.**

Read the value on each unit strip (careful with the negatives — $\lfloor x\rfloor=-2$ on $[-2,-1)$):
$$\underbrace{-2}_{[-2,-1)}+\underbrace{-1}_{[-1,0)}+\underbrace{0}_{[0,1)}+\underbrace{1}_{[1,2)}+
\underbrace{2}_{[2,3)}=0.$$
The negative strips cancel the positive ones exactly. *(Note this is **not** an odd function: $\lfloor
x\rfloor$ has no symmetry — you must read each strip.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 13

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2}\big\lceil x^{2}\big\rceil\,\mathrm dx$. &nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $4$ &nbsp;
**B** $7-\sqrt2-\sqrt3$ &nbsp; **C** $7$ &nbsp; **D** $10-\sqrt2-\sqrt3$ &nbsp; **E** $\tfrac{8}3$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a ceiling of a curve — irrational split points)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\lceil x^{2}\rceil$ jumps where $x^{2}$ passes an integer, at $x=\sqrt1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3$
:::

**Answer: B ($7-\sqrt2-\sqrt3$).**

**Step 1 — where does $\lceil x^{2}\rceil$ jump?** It changes each time $x^{2}$ passes an integer, i.e. at
$x=1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3$ (and $x=2$ ends the range). On $0<x^{2}\le n$ the ceiling is $n$:

| interval | $(0,1]$ | $(1,\sqrt2]$ | $(\sqrt2,\sqrt3]$ | $(\sqrt3,2]$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\lceil x^{2}\rceil$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| width | $1$ | $\sqrt2-1$ | $\sqrt3-\sqrt2$ | $2-\sqrt3$ |

**Step 2 — add value $\times$ width.**
$$1(1)+2(\sqrt2-1)+3(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)+4(2-\sqrt3)=1+2\sqrt2-2+3\sqrt3-3\sqrt2+8-4\sqrt3=7-\sqrt2-\sqrt3.$$

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
seg=[(0,1,1),(1,np.sqrt(2),2),(np.sqrt(2),np.sqrt(3),3),(np.sqrt(3),2,4)]
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.0))
xx=np.linspace(0,2,300); plt.plot(xx,xx**2,color='0.7',ls='--',label='y=x²')
for lo,hi,h in seg:
    plt.plot([lo,hi],[h,h],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2); plt.fill_between([lo,hi],[h,h],color='#2b6cb0',alpha=0.1)
for c in (np.sqrt(2),np.sqrt(3)): plt.axvline(c,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=0.8)
plt.xlim(0,2); plt.ylim(0,4.5); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title('⌈x²⌉ jumps at x=1, √2, √3 (irrational widths)',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}

:::

### Question 14

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}\lfloor x\rfloor\{x\}\,\mathrm dx$, where $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(floor times fractional part)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — on each strip $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is constant and $\{x\}$ is a fresh ramp $0\to1$
:::

**Answer: $3$.**

On $[k,\,k+1)$, $\lfloor x\rfloor=k$ (constant) and $\{x\}=x-k$ ramps from $0$ to $1$, so the strip
contributes $k\displaystyle\int_0^1 t\,\mathrm dt=\tfrac{k}2$. Summing $k=0,1,2,3$:
$$\int_0^4\lfloor x\rfloor\{x\}\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac02+\tfrac12+\tfrac22+\tfrac32=3.$$
*(In general $\int_0^n\lfloor x\rfloor\{x\}\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{n(n-1)}2=\tfrac{n(n-1)}4$.)*
:::

### Question 15

::: {.question}
Find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\lfloor5x\rfloor\,\mathrm dx$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a scaled floor)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\lfloor 5x\rfloor$ jumps at every fifth, giving five thin strips
:::

**Answer: $2$.**

$\lfloor5x\rfloor$ takes the values $0,1,2,3,4$ on the five strips $[0,\tfrac15),[\tfrac15,\tfrac25),\dots,
[\tfrac45,1)$, each of width $\tfrac15$:
$$\int_0^1\lfloor5x\rfloor\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac15(0+1+2+3+4)=\tfrac{10}5=2.$$
*(In general $\int_0^1\lfloor nx\rfloor\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac1n\cdot\tfrac{n(n-1)}2=\tfrac{n-1}2$.)*
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Memorise — floor & ceiling

- **$\lfloor x\rfloor$ rounds down** (careful: $\lfloor-2.3\rfloor=-3$); **$\lceil x\rceil$ rounds up**;
  $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in[0,1)$; for non-integers $\lceil x\rceil=\lfloor x\rfloor+1$.
- **Constant on each unit strip** $\Rightarrow$ integral $=$ **sum of strips**:
  $\int_0^n\lfloor x\rfloor=\tfrac{n(n-1)}2$, $\int_0^n\lceil x\rceil=\tfrac{n(n+1)}2$,
  $\int_0^n\{x\}=\tfrac n2$.
- **Strips that scale by a fixed factor** form a **geometric series** ($\sum2^{n}$, $\sum(2/3)^{k}$).
- **Finite floor sums:** group the terms sharing one floor value.
- **Equations:** put $\lfloor x\rfloor=n$ (integer), solve per strip, keep roots that land in their strip.
:::
